outcome: As of the latest sources read (to 24 Aug 2026) no accepted resolution exists: erdosproblems.com (last edited 16 Oct 2025), the Wikipedia lead (snapshot last edited 30 Jan 2026), the teorth/erdosproblems tracker (status open, last update 2025-08-31) and a 24 Aug 2026 arXiv paper all treat the problem as open. The only positive claims are an AfricArXiv preprint by Theophilus Agama (issued 9 Feb 2023, made available on the repository 22 Mar 2024), whose full text I could not read, and an anonymous comment on Tao's 2014 blog post (28 Jul 2024) pointing to a file I could not open. Conditional negative answers exist (Bombieri–Lang via Tao and Shaffaf; abc via Pasten; Lang's conjecture via Ascher–Braune–Turchet).
problem_asks: Whether there exists a set S of points in the Euclidean plane R² such that (i) S is dense in R² in the Euclidean topology (every open disc in R² meets S), and (ii) the distance between any two distinct points of S is rational. The statement asks only for the existence or non-existence of such an S; there is no second part. A dense rational-distance subset of a line or of a circle does not satisfy (i): such sets are dense only within the curve (Wikipedia; Erdős 1945 remark).

events.what_happened: Erdős's 1945 note, reported by Wikipedia as Anning and Erdős, 'Integral distances' (Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 51, 1945), and cited under the same title by Qiu (2026). The fetched PDF excerpt contains the remark 'It is easy to obtain a set which is dense on x^2+y^2=1/4 such that all the distances are rational', i.e. dense rational-distance subsets of one circle of rational radius. The excerpt is marked 'Received by the editors February 20, 1945'. The title and the attribution to Anning and Erdős come from the Wikipedia reference list and Qiu's reference list, not from the first page of the PDF, which I did not see. A search snippet reports that this note also records Ulam's question whether a dense rational-distance set exists in the plane; the excerpt I read does not contain that sentence, so I have not verified it.
events.delivers: A dense rational-distance subset of one circle (x^2+y^2=1/4). This is a partial result on a curve. It establishes nothing about a set dense in the whole plane.
events.remains: Whether a set dense in R² with all pairwise distances rational exists (all of problem_asks).

checked_by.who: Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (publication only; I did not verify a referee process or that the circle remark was checked)

events.directly_checkable: The circle remark is an explicit construction that a reader can check by parametrising the circle with rational points; the excerpt says only that it is 'easy'.
events.direction: Partial and positive, but only for a curve: it shows dense rational-distance subsets exist on a circle, which is the known obstruction to a planar answer being a curve.
events.object: A set dense on the circle x^2+y^2=1/4 with all pairwise distances rational. The note says it is easy to obtain; the construction itself was not in the excerpt I read.

events.what_happened: Kreisel and Kurz, 'There are integral heptagons, no three points on a line, no four on a circle' (arXiv:0804.1303, submitted 8 April 2008; Discrete Comput. Geom. 39 (2008) 786–790, per a search snippet). Two configurations of seven points in the plane with pairwise integral distances, no three collinear, no four concyclic. Answers a question of Erdős about finite configurations. The abstract concerns integral, not rational, distances, and finite sets.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 8 Apr 2008; journal version DCG 39 (2008) per search snippet.
events.delivers: Seven points with integral pairwise distances in general position. This is a finite, integral neighbouring question, not a dense rational-distance set.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (per search snippet; the journal page was not opened)

events.directly_checkable: Two explicit seven-point configurations; I read the abstract only and did not check coordinates.
events.direction: Neighbouring problem: finite integral configurations. It does not change whether a dense rational-distance set exists.
events.object: Two explicit configurations of seven points with integral pairwise distances, no three collinear and no four concyclic. Explicit (not stated as existence-only); coordinates not read.

events.what_happened: Solymosi and de Zeeuw, 'On a question of Erdős and Ulam' (arXiv:0806.3095, v1 submitted 18 June 2008; v2 14 Jan 2009; Discrete Comput. Geom. 43 (2010) 393–401). Main result per the abstract: no irreducible algebraic curve other than a line or a circle contains an infinite rational distance set. The proof uses Faltings' theorem (Mordell conjecture). The authors' v2 comment says v1 'didn't cover one special case'. The paper concerns curves and does not address a set dense in the plane.
events.revisions: v1 18 Jun 2008; v2 14 Jan 2009 (authors' comment: v1 'didn't cover one special case'); journal DCG 43(2) (2010) 393–401.
events.delivers: Unconditional classification for algebraic curves: infinite rational-distance subsets of an irreducible curve exist only on a line or a circle. Restricted to curves; nothing about a set dense in R².
events.remains: The planar question in full (all of problem_asks): the curve theorem says nothing about a set not contained in a curve.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal of record; referees not named in what I read

events.direction: Partial and unconditional, but on curves only; it leaves the planar density question untouched.

events.what_happened: Terence Tao, blog post 'The Erdos-Ulam problem, varieties of general type, and the Bombieri-Lang conjecture' (20 December 2014). Shows that an affirmative answer to the full Erdős–Ulam problem (a dense rational-distance set in R²) follows from the Bombieri–Lang conjecture: a general-type surface's rational points are not Zariski dense, applied to a blow-up surface that Tao shows is of general type. Tao says this demonstrates the conjecture's power and is not a practical unconditional route. The comment thread has about 22–23 comments (the page says 23) from 20 Dec 2014 to 28 Jul 2024. Shaffaf commented on 23 Dec 2014 and 3 Jan 2015. The 28 Jul 2024 comment is recorded as event mccallum-comment-2024.
events.revisions: Blog post 20 Dec 2014; comments through 28 Jul 2024. No edit history was shown in the text I read.
events.delivers: Conditional on Bombieri–Lang for surfaces of general type: no dense rational-distance set in R² (the answer 'no'). Unconditionally, nothing beyond Solymosi–de Zeeuw.
events.remains: Unconditionally, all of problem_asks. The conditional answer is 'no' only if Bombieri–Lang holds.

checked_by.qualification: Author of arXiv:1501.00159 (2014), which reaches the same conditional answer independently
checked_by.what_they_did: Commented on the post (23 Dec 2014; 3 Jan 2015); later published the paper. This is an independent route, not a check of Tao's argument.

events.doubts: Conditional: rests on the Bombieri–Lang conjecture (open) applied to surfaces of general type. Tao himself describes it as a demonstration of the conjecture's power, not an unconditional route.
events.direction: Conditional negative: a dense rational-distance set would contradict Bombieri–Lang for a general-type surface.

events.what_happened: Jafar Shaffaf, 'A solution of the Erdős–Ulam problem on rational distance sets assuming the Bombieri–Lang conjecture' (arXiv:1501.00159, v1 submitted 31 Dec 2014; Discrete Comput. Geom. 60 (2018) 283–293). Attaches to a finite rational distance set a 'distance surface' in P³ (z² equal to a product of squared distances to the points). The abstract says that under a mild condition this surface is always of general type, and that assuming Bombieri–Lang restricted to surfaces, the Erdős–Ulam problem is answered. The abstract summary also states that, combined with Solymosi–de Zeeuw, an infinite rational distance set has all but at most four points on a line or all but at most three on a circle. I could not tell from the abstract whether that final statement is conditional.
events.revisions: v1 31 Dec 2014; v2 7 Jan 2015; v3 20 Apr 2018 (adds an analysis of the singularity at infinity and a closing conjecture); journal DCG 60 (2018) 283–293.
events.delivers: Conditional on Bombieri–Lang for surfaces: no dense rational-distance set in R². Also, per the abstract summary, a structural statement about infinite rational-distance sets (line or circle with finitely many exceptions), whose conditionality I could not confirm.
events.remains: The unconditional planar question (all of problem_asks).

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 2018 (referees not named in what I read)

events.doubts: Conditional on Bombieri–Lang (surfaces). Version 3 (2018) adds material not in the earlier versions; I did not compare versions.
events.direction: Conditional negative (no dense set), with a conditional structural statement for infinite sets.

events.what_happened: Hector Pasten, 'Definability of Frobenius orbits and a result on rational distance sets', Monatsh. Math. 182 (2017) 99–126, DOI 10.1007/s00605-016-0973-2. Per Wikipedia and a SciSpace author-page search snippet, shows that the abc conjecture implies a negative answer to the Erdős–Ulam problem, by different methods from Shaffaf and Tao. The paper also has a model-theoretic result on meromorphic functions in positive characteristic. I did not read the paper: the Springer page redirected to a sign-in page. No arXiv preprint was found.
events.revisions: Monatsh. Math. 182 (2017) 99–126 per search snippet. No arXiv version found. The year 2016 is inferred from the DOI registration prefix and the 2017 volume; it is not confirmed from the publisher page.
events.delivers: Conditional on the abc conjecture: a negative answer (no dense rational-distance set), per secondary sources. The precise statement is not confirmed from the paper text.
events.doubts: Conditional on the abc conjecture. The paper itself was not read, so the conditional statement comes from secondary sources only.

events.what_happened: Kenneth Ascher, Lucas Braune and Amos Turchet, 'The Erdős–Ulam problem, Lang's conjecture, and uniformity' (arXiv:1901.02616, v1 9 Jan 2019; v2 17 Aug 2020; Bull. London Math. Soc. 52(6) (2020) 1053–1063, DOI 10.1112/blms.12381). Theorem 1.1, per the paper's introduction: assuming Lang's conjecture, there is a uniform bound on the cardinality of a rational distance set in general position (for an n-point set, no n−4 points on a line and no n−3 on a circle). The introduction says 'While this problem is still open' and records Shaffaf and Tao's conditional 'no'. The paper also includes a criterion for certain singular varieties to be of general type.
events.revisions: v1 9 Jan 2019; v2 17 Aug 2020 (exposition improved); journal BLMS 52(6) (2020) 1053–1063. The Wiley page returned HTTP 403, so the journal version was not read.
events.delivers: Conditional on Lang's conjecture: a uniform cardinality bound for rational-distance sets in general position. This does not establish a dense set and does not establish the 'no' answer on its own.
events.remains: The dense planar question unconditionally, and the uniform bound unconditionally (all of problem_asks).

checked_by.who: Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (2020; DOI from the arXiv record and a search snippet)

events.doubts: Conditional on Lang's conjecture (a conjecture about rational points on varieties of general type).
events.direction: Conditional bound in general position, pointing against dense sets only under Lang's conjecture.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'On the Erdős-Ulam problem in the plane' (AfricArXiv preprint, repository handle 1/1330, DOIs 10.14293/111.000/000057.v1 and 10.60763/africarxiv/1281; the PDF object count shows 9 pages). Abstract, quoted from the record page: 'In this paper we apply the method of compression to construct a dense set of points in the plane at rational distance from each other. We provide a positive solution to the Erdős–Ulam problem.' The record gives 'Issued 2023-02-09' and 'Made available on the repository 2024-03-22', with no version, journal or peer-review information. The PDF's text is in compressed streams that the tools available to me could not decode, so the construction, the density argument and the distance verification are unread. The abstract does not define how the method of compression is applied.
events.revisions: None shown on the record; DOI suffix '.v1'. The repository record was made available on 22 Mar 2024, which falls after the frozen revision date, so the first public appearance is ambiguous: the 2023 issue date predates the window, and the 2024 availability does not.
events.delivers: Per the abstract only: a positive answer, namely a dense set in R² all of whose pairwise distances are rational. Restrictions cannot be stated because the construction was not read.
events.remains: Per the abstract, nothing; the claim is not verified here.
events.time_since_posted: 3 years 8 months from the 2023 issue date; 2 years 6 months from the 2024 repository availability
events.directly_checkable: A dense set with rational pairwise distances can be stated concretely, but density in R² cannot be confirmed by finite computation, so the proof would be needed. Not read.
events.doubts: (1) Only the abstract and metadata were readable; the PDF body was not. (2) AfricArXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed or published. (3) A positive construction would be a counterexample to the conjectures on which the conditional 'no' results rest: Bombieri–Lang (Shaffaf, Tao), Lang's conjecture (Ascher–Braune–Turchet) and abc (Pasten). Wikipedia's lead says a positive solution 'would give counterexamples to the Bombieri–Lang and abc conjectures'. This is a signal for the later pass, not a verdict. (4) No review, comment or citation was found in my searches. The record page shows none. erdosproblems.com (last edited 16 Oct 2025) lists 0 comments and 0 proof claims, and the Wikipedia snapshot (30 Jan 2026) does not mention the claim. The one later paper I read in full, Qiu (2026), describes the problem as open and does not cite Agama.
events.direction: Positive claim: a dense planar set with all pairwise distances rational. This runs against the conditional literature, which points to 'no'.
events.object: Per the abstract only: a dense subset of R² all of whose pairwise distances are rational, claimed to be built by 'the method of compression' (not defined in the abstract). Whether the object is explicit or non-constructive is not stated. The content was not read.

events.what_happened: Rachel Greenfeld, Marina Iliopoulou and Sarah Peluse, 'On integer distance sets' (arXiv:2401.10821; v1 19 Jan 2024; v2 7 Mar 2024; v3 25 Aug 2025). Per the abstract: any integer distance set in the Euclidean plane is either very sparse or has nearly all its points on a single line or circle, with consequences for diameters and sizes in bounded squares. The abstract does not mention rational distance sets, Erdős–Ulam, or Agama, Shaffaf or Tao. I read the abstract page only.
events.delivers: Integer (not rational) distance sets in the plane: sparse, or almost entirely on a line or circle. A neighbouring question; it does not bear on a dense set with all pairwise distances rational.
events.direction: Neighbouring question: integer distances. No direction on the rational dense question.

events.what_happened: Pietro Corvaja, Amos Turchet and Umberto Zannier, 'Rational distances from given rational points in the plane' (arXiv:2403.02030; v1 4 Mar 2024; v2 10 Dec 2024, a major rewriting; Geometriae Dedicata 219.4 (2025), DOI 10.1007/s10711-025-01019-0). Studies points of the plane whose distances to r prescribed points are all rational. For r = 3 they give explicit, congruence-checkable conditions for density of such points in the real topology, always satisfied for rational fixed points. For r ≥ 4 the points correspond to rational points on a surface of general type, conjecturally not Zariski dense, and the authors say they lack methods to prove that. The abstract does not mention the Erdős–Ulam problem.
events.revisions: v1 4 Mar 2024; v2 10 Dec 2024 (major rewriting); journal Geom. Dedicata 219.4 (2025).
events.delivers: A different question: rational distances from fixed points, not a set whose pairwise distances are all rational. It establishes nothing about the Erdős–Ulam set.
events.direction: Different question (distances to fixed points). No direction on the Erdős–Ulam set.

events.what_happened: An anonymous comment on Tao's 2014 blog post, dated 28 Jul 2024, signed 'Duncan McCallum' (the comment gives an email address, which I have not recorded). It says the author first learned of the problem from Václav Chvátal of McGill in 1978 and offers 'a solution by constructing a set that meets the Erdos-Ulam conditions'. It links to a Google Drive file named '24-07-21 erdos.pdf'. The Drive page requires sign-in and returned no text, so the construction is unread. Searches found no arXiv or journal posting by this author and no 1978 record linking the author or Chvátal to the problem.
events.delivers: Unknown. A claimed positive construction whose content I could not read.
events.remains: Unknown. If the claim holds, nothing; if not, all of problem_asks.
events.directly_checkable: The linked file, if accessible, would have to be checked for density and for the rational distances. Not accessible to me.
events.doubts: Anonymous or signed-only comment; the linked file was inaccessible; no preprint or journal posting found; erdosproblems.com lists 0 proof claims; the one later paper I read in full (Qiu 2026) does not cite it. The 1978 attribution is unverified.
events.object: Claimed: a set meeting the Erdős–Ulam conditions, dense with all pairwise distances rational. Its description is in the linked Google Drive file, which I could not open.
people: Duncan McCallum (name from the signature; identity not verified)

events.what_happened: Junkai Qiu (School of Mathematical Sciences, Dalian University of Technology, per the arXiv HTML), 'Infinite rational distance sets in affine general position: constructions in every dimension' (arXiv:2608.23529; v1 submitted 24 Aug 2026; math.CO, cross-listed math.MG). For every d ≥ 1 constructs a countably infinite X_d ⊂ R^d in affine general position with all pairwise distances rational; for odd d the set can be in general position. The even-dimensional construction lies on a single sphere, so the d = 2 instance lies on a circle. The paper says the Erdős–Ulam problem 'asks whether the plane contains a dense rational distance set and remains open'. I read the HTML version in two passes and found no statement on AI, LLM or model assistance. The PDF text was unreadable.
events.delivers: Countably infinite rational-distance sets in affine general position in every dimension. In the plane the construction lies on a circle, so it is not dense and it does not bear on the planar question. The paper treats the Erdős–Ulam problem as open.
events.directly_checkable: The d = 2 instance is a countable subset of a circle with rational distances. I did not check the proof.
events.direction: Neighbouring: infinite sets, dimension by dimension. For the plane it is on a circle and cuts no way on dense planar sets. It explicitly states the problem is open.
events.object: Explicit-looking construction per the paper's description (Chebyshev square decompositions, a divided-difference factorisation of the affine determinant, stereographic projection for odd d). For d = 2 the countable set lies on a circle. I did not verify it.

disputes.summary: Ulam's question is dated to 1945 in Shaffaf's abstract summary and in the 1945 Erdős note context, and to 1946 in the Wikipedia article and in the Ascher–Braune–Turchet introduction. Not resolved here.

Agama (2023) claims a positive solution. erdosproblems.com (last edited 16 Oct 2025), the teorth/erdosproblems tracker (status open, last update 2025-08-31), the Wikipedia lead (snapshot 30 Jan 2026), Ascher–Braune–Turchet (2019) and Qiu (2026) all state the problem open. None of these sources addresses the Agama claim.
The 28 Jul 2024 comment attributes the problem's origin to Václav Chvátal (McGill, 1978) and gives the author as Duncan McCallum. Neither could be verified.

summary: The problem is open in every source I could read that speaks to its current status: erdosproblems.com #212 (open; last edited 16 Oct 2025; 0 comments, 0 proof claims; Lean formal statement in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures marked research open with a sorry in the statement, which is not a proof), the teorth/erdosproblems tracker (open; last update 2025-08-31; its formalized flag reads 'yes' while formal_status reads 'unformalized'), the Wikipedia article (lead: 'While the answer to this question is still open'; snapshot last edited 30 Jan 2026), and Qiu's arXiv paper of 24 Aug 2026, which says the problem 'remains open'. The record holds twelve events. Two are positive claims. The first is Theophilus Agama's AfricArXiv preprint (issued 9 Feb 2023; made available on the repository 22 Mar 2024), whose abstract says 'We provide a positive solution to the Erdős–Ulam problem' via 'the method of compression'. I could not read its PDF text, so its construction and its density and distance claims are unverified. Its record shows no review, and I found no comment or citation; the one later paper I read in full does not cite it. The second is an anonymous comment on Tao's 2014 post (28 Jul 2024) signed 'Duncan McCallum', which offers a solution in a linked Google Drive file I could not open. Close call on Agama's date: if the 2023 issue date is the first public posting, the event predates the window; if the 22 Mar 2024 repository availability is the first public appearance, it falls inside. The conditional negative results are Tao (2014) and Shaffaf (2014/2018), conditional on Bombieri–Lang for surfaces; Pasten (2016/2017), conditional on abc, which I took from Wikipedia and a search snippet rather than the paper; and Ascher–Braune–Turchet (2019), a uniform bound in general position under Lang's conjecture. Solymosi–de Zeeuw (2008/2010) is unconditional but covers only curves, and Ulam's question appears in the 1945 Erdős note context. The other events are neighbouring questions: Kreisel–Kurz (finite integral sets), Greenfeld–Iliopoulou–Peluse (integer distance sets, 19 Jan 2024), Corvaja–Turchet–Zannier (distances to fixed points), and Qiu 2026 (infinite sets in general position, on a circle in the plane). I found no unconditional progress on the planar question in the window. AI: none of the twelve events names an AI system, and the AI-specific searches found no AI credit for rational-distance progress. The AI results that did come up concern other problems: the OpenAI unit-distance disproof (May 2026), Erdős #659 with Gemini 3 Pro, and #728 and #281 with GPT-5.2 Pro. I did not record those as events because they do not bear on this problem. The Quanta article of 3 Aug 2026 on AI and Erdős problems does not mention this problem.
competing_reading: The Agama claim could be a real resolution. The conditional literature shows only that a dense set would contradict Bombieri–Lang, Lang's conjecture, or abc; none is proved, so a construction is not ruled out in principle. On that reading the problem's status changed in 2023 (or 2024 if the repository date is taken), and the Agama preprint is the event that counts. The opposing reading treats an abstract-only, unreviewed claim that contradicts the conditional literature, with no uptake in more than three years and no entry on the problem's own status page, as no event. Both readings rest on the same facts; the difference is how much weight the silence and the conflict carry.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A readable copy of the Agama PDF, to see whether the construction gives a dense set with all pairwise distances rational, whether 'compression' is defined, and whether any AI or software is acknowledged. (2) A journal decision on Agama, or a named expert's written verification or refutation. (3) The contents of the linked Google Drive file '24-07-21 erdos.pdf' from the McCallum comment. (4) Dated erdosproblems.com history for #212 after 20 Oct 2025, covering status and proof-claim entries, and the tracker's current entry for 212. (5) Google Scholar or Semantic Scholar cited-by lists for the Agama record and for Pasten (2017), which I could not access.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether a dense planar rational-distance set exists. Results conditional on Bombieri–Lang, abc or Lang (Tao, Shaffaf, Pasten, Ascher–Braune–Turchet) reduce the question to unproven conjectures, so their scope is none. Results on curves, integer distances, finite configurations, distances to fixed points, or infinite sets lying on a circle (1945 note, Solymosi–de Zeeuw, Kreisel–Kurz, Greenfeld–Iliopoulou–Peluse, Corvaja–Turchet–Zannier, Qiu) answer changed questions, so they are variants. The only two whole-problem claims are Agama and McCallum. Both are positive constructions that nobody has read, and both meet several F10 signals together: a landmark problem, years of silence, unvetted venues, and later status sources that still call the problem open. Both are marked not_credible. The statement asks whether such a set exists, so a claimed dense set is a witness and the direction is 'confirmed' relative to the question as asked, even though it runs against the conjectured 'no'.
judgement.doubts: Agama's date cannot be placed. It was issued 9 Feb 2023, but it was only made available on the repository on 22 Mar 2024, and the record cannot say which was its first public appearance. after_snapshot is null. Neither claim's content was read: the Agama PDF could not be decoded and the McCallum file was behind a sign-in wall. The not_credible calls therefore rest on context, not on any identified error. Conditional results answered 'none' as reductions to unproven conditions.
